questions.question: Q1. Describe the Rutherford (gold-foil) experiment and its conclusion about the nucleus.
questions.answer: α-particles fired at thin gold foil: most passed through (atom mostly empty), a few deflected, a very few (~1 in 20 000) bounced back. Conclusion: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m) contains nearly all the mass and positive charge.
questions.shortcut: Most pass → empty; some back-scatter → tiny dense + nucleus.
questions.example: The nucleus is ~100 000× smaller than the atom.

questions.question: Q2. State the formula for nuclear radius and nuclear density.
questions.answer: Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1.2×10⁻¹⁵ m). Since volume ∝ R³ ∝ A and mass ∝ A, nuclear density ρ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁷ kg/m³, essentially independent of A (nearly constant for all nuclei).
questions.example: A uranium and a lithium nucleus have almost the same density.

questions.question: Q3. Write Einstein's mass-energy relation and the u–MeV conversion.
questions.answer: E = mc². Using 1 u = 931 MeV/c², a mass defect of 1 u corresponds to 931 MeV of binding energy.
questions.example: A 2 u defect gives 1862 MeV of energy.

questions.question: Q4. Define mass defect and binding energy.
questions.answer: Mass defect Δm is the difference between the total mass of the separated nucleons and the actual nuclear mass: Δm = [Zm_p + (A−Z)m_n] − m_nucleus. Binding energy BE = Δm·c² (the energy needed to disassemble the nucleus). ▥ 24.1–24.4 Nucleus, Density & Mass-Energy  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Alpha vs Beta vs Gamma Radiation Nuclear Density Table Mass Defect vs Mass-Energy Equivalence ▣ 24.5 Packing Fraction & BE per Nucleon
questions.example: He-4: 2p+2n mass > He-4 mass; the difference is the BE.

questions.question: Q5. Define packing fraction and what it indicates.
questions.answer: Packing fraction = [Zm_p + (A−Z)m_n − m_nucleus]/A, roughly the fractional mass defect per nucleon. It indicates how tightly bound the nucleons are; a larger (more negative) value means a more stable nucleus.
questions.shortcut: PF ∝ (mass defect)/A; more negative → more stable.
questions.example: Medium nuclei have the most negative packing fraction.

questions.question: Q6. Explain the BE/nucleon curve and why iron is the most stable.
questions.answer: BE per nucleon rises from H, peaks near A ≈ 56 (iron group, ~8.8 MeV), then slowly falls for heavy nuclei. Iron has the maximum BE/nucleon, so it is the most tightly bound (most stable); light nuclei can fuse (gain BE), heavy can fission (gain BE).
questions.shortcut: Peak at A≈56 (Fe); max stability; light → fuse, heavy → split.
questions.example: Fusion of light H releases energy; fission of U-235 releases energy.

questions.question: Q7. Find the binding energy of helium-4 (mass = 4.0015 u; m_p=1.0073, m_n=1.0087 u).
questions.answer: Mass of parts = 2(1.0073)+2(1.0087) = 4.0320 u. Δm = 4.0320 − 4.0015 = 0.0305 u. BE = 0.0305×931 ≈ 28.4 MeV; BE/nucleon ≈ 7.1 MeV. ▥ 24.5 Packing Fraction & BE per Nucleon  —  Compare / Contrast Tables BE per Nucleon Curve: Key Reading ▣ 24.6–24.7 Creation/Annihilation & Fission/Fusion

questions.question: Q8. Explain particle creation and annihilation (pair production/annihilation).
questions.answer: A photon of sufficient energy (≥2mc²) can convert into a particle–antiparticle pair (pair production). When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate into photons (e⁻+e⁺→2γ). Mass and energy are interconverted via E = mc².
questions.example: An electron–positron pair annihilates into two 511 keV gamma rays.

questions.question: Q9. Differentiate nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
questions.answer: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into lighter fragments, releasing energy (chain reaction, e.g. U-235 + n → Ba + Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV). Fusion: light nuclei combine into a heavier one, releasing energy (e.g. 4 H → He + energy, powers the Sun). Both follow E = Δm c².
questions.shortcut: Fission: heavy → light; Fusion: light → heavy. Both release BE.
questions.example: Fission in reactors/bombs; fusion in the Sun/H-bombs.

questions.question: Q10. Why is energy released in both fission and fusion?
questions.answer: In both, the products have a higher BE/nucleon than the reactants; the 'missing' mass (mass defect) is converted to energy (E = Δm c²). Fusion of light nuclei climbs toward the Fe peak; fission of heavy nuclei also climbs toward it.
questions.shortcut: Products bind more tightly → mass defect → energy.
questions.example: A small mass loss gives a huge energy (c² factor).

questions.question: Q11. Explain a chain reaction and what is needed to sustain it.
questions.answer: A chain reaction occurs when neutrons from one fission induce further fissions. It is self-sustaining when the reproduction factor (avg neutrons causing new fissions per fission) ≥ 1; <1 dies out, >1 grows (supercritical). Moderators slow neutrons; control rods absorb them.
questions.shortcut: Sustained when # new fissions ≥ previous; moderator slows, rods absorb.
questions.example: U-235 + slow neutron is most easily fissionable.

questions.question: Q12. What is the advantage of fusion over fission (environment)?
questions.answer: Fusion of light isotopes (e.g. D-T) produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, no high-level spent fuel, and the fuel (deuterium, lithium) is very abundant; it also has no risk of a meltdown. Energy density per fuel mass is higher. ▥ 24.6–24.7 Creation/Annihilation & Fission/Fusion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Nuclear Fusion vs Fission Creation vs Annihilation of Matter PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Less waste, abundant fuel, no meltdown; huge energy.
questions.example: The Sun has fused hydrogen for billions of years.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the binding energy from the mass defect.
theoryItems.answer: Mass defect Δm = [Zm_p + (A−Z)m_n] − m_nucleus (the 'missing' mass). Binding energy BE = Δm·c²; using 1 u = 931 MeV, BE = Δm(in u) × 931 MeV. This is the energy needed to disassemble the nucleus into its nucleons.
theoryItems.shortcut: Δm = Σparts − m_nucleus ; BE = Δm×931 MeV.
theoryItems.example: He-4 has Δm ≈ 0.0305 u → BE ≈ 28.4 MeV.

theoryItems.question: [State] T2. State the formula for nuclear radius and nuclear density.
theoryItems.answer: Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1.2×10⁻¹⁵ m). Since volume ∝ R³ ∝ A and mass ∝ A, the nuclear density is nearly constant, ρ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁷ kg/m³, independent of A (all nuclei have roughly the same density).
theoryItems.example: A uranium and a lithium nucleus have nearly the same density.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T3. Compare nuclear fission and fusion (with advantages/disadvantages).
theoryItems.answer: Fission: heavy → light (chain reaction, U-235), ~200 MeV/event, produces radioactive waste, no high-temperature requirement (feasible today). Fusion: light → heavy (needs extreme T to overcome Coulomb barrier), ~4× energy per fuel mass, no long-lived waste, but harder to control (experimental).
theoryItems.shortcut: Fission: ready today, waste; Fusion: cleaner, harder.
theoryItems.example: Both move toward the iron BE peak.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain the Rutherford (gold-foil) experiment and its conclusions about the nucleus.
theoryItems.answer: α-particles were fired at thin gold foil: most passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space), a few deflected at large angles, a very few bounced back. Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m), far smaller than the atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m).
theoryItems.shortcut: Most pass → empty; some back-scatter → tiny dense + nucleus.
theoryItems.example: The nucleus is ~100 000× smaller than the atom.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain mass number, atomic number and isotopes.
theoryItems.answer: The atomic number Z is the number of protons (defines the element); the mass number A is protons + neutrons; the number of neutrons is N = A − Z. Isotopes are the same Z, different N (same element, different A), differing in mass and stability.
theoryItems.shortcut: Z: element; A: total nucleons; N = A−Z ; isotope = same Z, different N.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain Einstein's mass-energy relation and pair production/annihilation.
theoryItems.answer: Mass and energy are equivalent: E = mc². A photon with energy ≥ 2mc² can produce a particle–antiparticle pair (pair production); when a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate into photons of total energy 2mc². This underlies creation/annihilation processes.
theoryItems.shortcut: E = mc² ; γ → pair if E ≥ 2mc² ; pair → γγ.
theoryItems.example: Electron–positron annihilation gives two 511 keV photons.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the BE/nucleon curve and why iron is the most stable.
theoryItems.answer: BE per nucleon rises from H, peaks near A ≈ 56 (iron group, ~8.8 MeV), then slowly falls for heavy nuclei. Iron has the maximum BE/nucleon, so it is the most tightly bound (most stable). Light nuclei can fuse to gain BE; heavy nuclei can fission to gain BE; both move toward the iron peak.
theoryItems.example: Fusion of light H and fission of U-235 both release energy.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain nuclear fission and a chain reaction.
theoryItems.answer: In fission, a heavy nucleus (e.g. U-235) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two lighter fragments plus 2–3 neutrons and ~200 MeV; these neutrons can induce more fissions. If the reproduction factor (new fissions per old fission) is ≥ 1, the chain reaction is sustained; a moderator slows neutrons and control rods absorb them to regulate it.
theoryItems.shortcut: Sustained when ≥1 new fission per old fission; moderator + rods.
theoryItems.example: Reactor control uses boron/cadmium control rods.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T9. Explain nuclear fusion and the proton-proton chain in the Sun.
theoryItems.answer: In fusion, light nuclei combine into a heavier one with higher BE/nucleon, releasing the mass defect as energy. In the Sun, the proton-proton chain fuses four protons into a helium-4 nucleus (via two deuterons), releasing ~26.7 MeV and positrons/neutrinos. This is the Sun's energy source (and of H-bombs).
theoryItems.shortcut: Light + light → heavier + energy (toward Fe peak).
theoryItems.example: The Sun's pp chain: 4p → He-4 + energy + 2ν + 2e⁺.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T10. Professor: 'Why does fission of U-235 need slow neutrons?'
theoryItems.answer: U-235 is fissionable only with slow (thermal) neutrons; a fast neutron has too much kinetic energy and is more likely to pass through without being captured. A moderator (water, graphite) slows the neutrons to thermal energies, making fission far more likely.
theoryItems.example: Moderators slow neutrons to make fission probable.

▣ 24.1–24.4 Nucleus, Density & Mass-Energy
Q1. Describe the Rutherford (gold-foil) experiment and its conclusion about the nucleus.

Answer:  α-particles fired at thin gold foil: most passed through (atom mostly empty), a few deflected, a very few (~1 in 20 000) bounced back. Conclusion: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m) contains nearly all the mass and positive charge.
⚡ Shortcut:  Most pass → empty; some back-scatter → tiny dense + nucleus.
Example:  The nucleus is ~100 000× smaller than the atom.
Q2. State the formula for nuclear radius and nuclear density.

Answer:  Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1.2×10⁻¹⁵ m). Since volume ∝ R³ ∝ A and mass ∝ A, nuclear density ρ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁷ kg/m³, essentially independent of A (nearly constant for all nuclei).
⚡ Shortcut:  R = 1.2A^(1/3) fm ; ρ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁷ kg/m³ (constant).
Example:  A uranium and a lithium nucleus have almost the same density.
Q3. Write Einstein's mass-energy relation and the u–MeV conversion.
Answer:  E = mc². Using 1 u = 931 MeV/c², a mass defect of 1 u corresponds to 931 MeV of binding energy.
⚡ Shortcut:  1 u = 931 MeV/c² ; E = Δm·931 MeV.
Example:  A 2 u defect gives 1862 MeV of energy.
Q4. Define mass defect and binding energy.

Answer:  Mass defect Δm is the difference between the total mass of the separated nucleons and the actual nuclear mass: Δm = [Zm_p + (A−Z)m_n] − m_nucleus. Binding energy BE = Δm·c² (the energy needed to disassemble the nucleus).
⚡ Shortcut:  BE = Δm·c² = Δm(u)×931 MeV.
Example:  He-4: 2p+2n mass > He-4 mass; the difference is the BE.

Answer:  BE per nucleon rises from H, peaks near A ≈ 56 (iron group, ~8.8 MeV), then slowly falls for heavy nuclei. Iron has the maximum BE/nucleon, so it is the most tightly bound (most stable); light nuclei can fuse (gain BE), heavy can fission (gain BE).
⚡ Shortcut:  Peak at A≈56 (Fe); max stability; light → fuse, heavy → split.

Q8. Explain particle creation and annihilation (pair production/annihilation).

Answer:  A photon of sufficient energy (≥2mc²) can convert into a particle–antiparticle pair (pair production). When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate into photons (e⁻+e⁺→2γ). Mass and energy are interconverted via E = mc².
⚡ Shortcut:  γ→pair if E≥2mc² ; particle+antiparticle→γγ.
Example:  An electron–positron pair annihilates into two 511 keV gamma rays.
Q9. Differentiate nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.

Answer:  Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into lighter fragments, releasing energy (chain reaction, e.g. U-235 + n → Ba + Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV). Fusion: light nuclei combine into a heavier one, releasing energy (e.g. 4 H → He + energy, powers the Sun). Both follow E = Δm c².
⚡ Shortcut:  Fission: heavy → light; Fusion: light → heavy. Both release BE.
Example:  Fission in reactors/bombs; fusion in the Sun/H-bombs.
Q10. Why is energy released in both fission and fusion?

Answer:  In both, the products have a higher BE/nucleon than the reactants; the 'missing' mass (mass defect) is converted to energy (E = Δm c²). Fusion of light nuclei climbs toward the Fe peak; fission of heavy nuclei also climbs toward it.
⚡ Shortcut:  Products bind more tightly → mass defect → energy.
Example:  A small mass loss gives a huge energy (c² factor).
Q11. Explain a chain reaction and what is needed to sustain it.

Answer:  A chain reaction occurs when neutrons from one fission induce further fissions. It is self-sustaining when the reproduction factor (avg neutrons causing new fissions per fission) ≥ 1; <1 dies out, >1 grows (supercritical). Moderators slow neutrons; control rods absorb them.
⚡ Shortcut:  Sustained when # new fissions ≥ previous; moderator slows, rods absorb.
Example:  U-235 + slow neutron is most easily fissionable.
Q12. What is the advantage of fusion over fission (environment)?

Answer:  Fusion of light isotopes (e.g. D-T) produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, no high-level spent fuel, and the fuel (deuterium, lithium) is very abundant; it also has no risk of a meltdown. Energy density per fuel mass is higher.
⚡ Shortcut:  Less waste, abundant fuel, no meltdown; huge energy.
Example:  The Sun has fused hydrogen for billions of years.
